title: Gaia Alari's Lilting Animations are Drawn Frame by Frame
description: Gaia Alari’s works are defined by a distinct, effervescent visual language. Made from thousands of handmade drawings on paper, the artist’s elabor
body:
Gaia Alari’s works are defined by a distinct, effervescent visual language. Made from thousands of handmade drawings on paper, the artist’s elaborate animations put on strikingly tactile performances as fleeting marks of oil pastel and charcoal dance across the screen.
Meandering botanical forms, gestural bodies, and sweeping birds converge into fluid loops that create a rhythm reminiscent of a stream of consciousness. Whether Alari is collaborating with a brand, exploring personal interests, or creating static illustrations, it’s clear that each piece tells a distinct story. Watch more from the artist on Vimeo and keep up with her explorations on Instagram.

title: Tomás Saraceno Returns to the Past to Envision a More Just Future
description: How might we visualize the inextricable web of space, time, and matter, enormous concepts that are so systemic they can almost become abstract? Re
body:
How might we visualize the inextricable web of space, time, and matter, enormous concepts that are so systemic they can almost become abstract? Rendering these connections in a tangible, accessible, and even participatory manner continues to ground Tomás Saraceno’s multidisciplinary practice. Born in Argentina and based in Berlin, the artist plays with scale and spectacle to draw our attention to the life-giving ecosystems in which we’re all bound, merging art, architecture, and science into alluring works.
At Haus der Kunst, Saraceno’s ecological and collaborative projects take center stage for a sweeping presentation titled Ancestral Futures. Spanning more than two decades, the solo exhibition emerges from the central premise that the knowledge we’ve gained in the past is critical to understanding and creating our shared tomorrow. 
Tomás Saraceno in collaboration, ‘Ancestral Futures’ exhibition view at Haus der Kunst München (2026). Photo by Agostino Osio, © Haus der Kunst München
Called “the art world’s favorite arachnophile,” Saraceno frequently returns to the spider and its web as a metaphor for and example of the networks that undergird life. Interactive installations invite visitors to crawl through sprawling structures, while the decade-long Webs of At-tent(s)ion series welcomes several species of spiders into the museum to spin their sticky structures inside boxes. Continually returning to the web is a clear reminder that we’re all connected to one another and that nature’s processes are cyclical.
Saraceno also adapts his interest in solar-powered air balloons for the museum. An immersive cavern made of crowd-sourced plastic bags inflates with the help of willing visitors who ride stationary bicycles to power the project. Others can wander inside, where they become enveloped by a colorful patchwork of brands and remnants of humanity’s culture of disposability and consumerism.
Perhaps the most impressive works in the exhibition are those created as part of Saraceno’s ongoing collaboration with Indigenous communities of Red Atacama, in the basin of Salinas Grandes in northwestern Argentina. Eleven weavers loaned their handmade blankets, which are presented together as a vibrant, soft space for lounging at the show’s opening. Immersion into the landscape of Salinas Grandes follows with galleries filled with sand, water, salt, and more.
Several works reference The Sanctuary of Water, the multi-pronged project Saraceno and the people of Salinas Grandes are undertaking together. The collaboration, the museum says, “emerges in solidarity with the communities’resistance to lithium mining in one of the world’s largest lithium-rich regions. Their struggle highlights the continuing legacy of colonial exploitation: While international corporations profit from resources such as lithium—essential for technologies including electric cars—the environmental and social costs are borne by local communities.”



As a permanent land work, “The Sanctuary of Water” is organized around a large reflective pond that captures the sky above, skewing boundaries between land and air. “In our worldview,” says the collaborative project’s website, “Pacha names the inseparable weave of space, time, and matter. It is one living body, sustained by the water that flows through them all.”
If you’re in Munich, you can see Ancestral Futures through February 7. Otherwise, explore more of the artist’s collaboration with the communities of Salinas Grandes on the project’s website.
“The Sanctuary of Water” (2026). Photo © Studio Tomás Saraceno
Tomás Saraceno in collaboration, ‘Ancestral Futures’ exhibition view at Haus der Kunst München (2026). Photo by Agostino Osio, © Haus der Kunst München
“El Santuario del Agua Salinas Grandes” (2026). Photo © Studio Tomás Saraceno
“When the Llama Drinks from the Stars and the Spider Weaves Cycles of Life, Where the Sky Touches the Earth and Time Expands Like Salt, the Sanctuary of Water Are Fair Clouds on the Horizon” (2025). Photo © Studio Tomás Saraceno
“El Santuario del Agua Salinas Grandes” (2026). Photo © Studio Tomás Saraceno

title: Wild Hijinx and Hilarious Happenstance Reign in the 2026 Comedy Wildlife Awards
description: The year’s best roundup of the funniest animal photos is back with its list of 2026 finalists, taking on a kind of blooper reel-like quality with
body:
The year’s best roundup of the funniest animal photos is back with its list of 2026 finalists, taking on a kind of blooper reel-like quality with some of the goofiest happenstances and candid moments photographers captured. Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards 2026 celebrates the wild, wonderful, and wily in habitats around the world.
From Tanner Mansell’s “Spicy Orangutan” snapped in Borneo to a damselfly appearing to wave at British photographer Lee Frost through a window in a nibbled leaf, this year’s top contenders are not only silly, but immanently relatable, illustrating how for all of our differences, we all share this incredible planet.
Tanner Mansell, “Spicy Orangutan”
At more than 10,000 photos, the competition received its highest ever number of entries this year from photographers in 112 countries. “What began as a small effort to raise awareness of wildlife conservation has grown into something far bigger than we ever imagined,” says awards co-founder Tom Sullam. “We use humour to get people to feel empathy towards wildlife, and it’s that empathy that creates behavioural change for the better.”
Nikon will announce the competition winners on December 8. In the meantime, see all 40 finalists, plus portfolios, videos, and youth submissions on the contests’s website. Additionally, cast your vote for the Sterna People’s Choice Award.

title: Three NYC Museum Unions Ratify Contracts, Averting Strikes
description:
News
                Workers at the American Folk Art Museum, Brooklyn Museum, and Guggenheim Museum had bargained for higher pa
body:
News
                Workers at the American Folk Art Museum, Brooklyn Museum, and Guggenheim Museum had bargained for higher pay and better working conditions. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Workers at the American Folk Art Museum rally outside the institution’s annual gala at the Mandarin Oriental in Manhattan on May 6, 2026. (photos Aaron Short/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            After months of collective bargaining and looming strikes, unionized staff at the Brooklyn Museum and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum have ratified their second contracts with their respective institutions, while the American Folk Art Museum (AFAM) union is celebrating the ratification of its first contract with the museum. These developments come after the Whitney Museum of American Art, Brooklyn Museum, and AFAM unions jointly voted to authorize strike action last month if a tentative agreement could not be reached, falling in line with the Guggenheim union, which had voted in favor of a strike at the end of June.However, unionized Whitney staff have set a strike deadline of Monday, October 5, ahead of the press and VIP previews and opening date for the museum's Roy Lichtenstein retrospective that week, which they are prepared to picket throughout. Ahead of their second contracts, the Brooklyn Museum and the Guggenheim were under intense scrutiny early into 2025 after initiating sweeping staff cuts, which they attributed to mounting financial constraints.

title: British Museum to Provide Bayeux Tapestry Audio Tour After Lawsuit
description:
News
                Yusuf Ali Osman, a man with no sight, filed a suit against the museum under the UK's anti-discrimination Eq
body:
News
                Yusuf Ali Osman, a man with no sight, filed a suit against the museum under the UK's anti-discrimination Equality Act.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Unrelated London man outside the British Museum in London, where the Bayeux Tapestry is on display (photo Richard Baker / In Pictures via Getty Images)
    
        
            The British Museum will provide audio tour options for its Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after a blind patron pursued legal action against the London institution last week, according to the BBC.Yusuf Ali Osman, a man from Croydon with no sight, accused the museum of violating the Equality Act 2010 by not offering audio tours of the exhibition, his legal representatives said in a statement shared with Hyperallergic. Under the Equality Act, which is the central anti-discrimination law in Great Britain, individuals are protected against acts such as ageism, ableism, and racism in the workplace and in other environments.The museum had allegedly told Osman that the exhibit prioritized self-guided visits over programmed tours due to its restricted visitor capacity. To avoid light exposure damage to the millennium-old work, the museum must limit the number of people who can enter the gallery."I want to be able to visit the Bayeux Tapestry and experience it for myself," Osman said in a statement shared with Hyperallergic. Apart from damages, he seeks a declaration from the museum acknowledging its discrimination against him, and an order requiring policy amendments and disability awareness training for museum staff.

title: Mala Iqbal Paints the Space We Share With Strangers
description:
Art Review
                Her new paintings remind us that the world is a room we share with strangers, most of whom are lookin
body:
Art Review
                Her new paintings remind us that the world is a room we share with strangers, most of whom are looking elsewhere. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Mala Iqbal’s “Subway Riders” (2026) by the front windows of JJ Murphy gallery on Manhattan's Lower East Side (all photos Hrag Vartanian/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            Figures jostle the surface of every Mala Iqbal canvas with the energy of a great metropolis. Many are bathed in an orange and yellow glow, a tinge of artifice for people who live under electric light, places where even the sun isn't enough. Some of the paintings forgo that effect, like "Through the Curtains” (2026). Left to right, we see a scene of collapse, which is obscured by a tulle curtain rendering like a faded negative; a figure reacts, almost numbly; and ultimately another curtain finishes the scene with a pictograph-like pattern — life, transformed by a screen, experienced by someone, and turned into an indecipherable language. I view it as a metaphor for how our screens deliver collapse and violence with every scroll, faster than we can process it.Mala Iqbal, “Through the Curtains” (2026)Each work is about the construction of reality, sometimes cobbled together, other times layered and occasionally philosophized through the arrangement of images, figures, and signs. Social realism casts a long shadow, though the mood is closer to Matisse's ease. Her “Times Square” (2026) has the chalky palette of Ben Shahn, which gives the image its own terroir, and it never sours into despair.Many of the paintings take place in subways, places where false intimacies give us the illusion of knowing. But the artist never drops the urban masks we wear as we stare into faces that look away or are obstructed and rendered into shapely flourishes, bringing to light strange but enticing surfaces. One figure is recognizable, that of the painter’s partner, artist Angela Dufresne, in “Subway Riders” (2026), who herself seems to be recording something of her own, staring towards us but not at us, reminding us how our own relationships depict us as much as we depict them.Detail of Mala Iqbal, “Transparent Friend” (2025)

title: Francis Lee Rogers, Painter and Avid Birdwatcher, Found Dead in Central Park
description:
News
                The 63-year-old artist, who was unhoused, was known as the “Grandma Moses of Central Park” for her various
body:
News
                The 63-year-old artist, who was unhoused, was known as the “Grandma Moses of Central Park” for her various depictions of its fauna and flora. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Francis Lee Rogers holds up one of her paintings (photo via Facebook)Francis Lee Rogers, a 63-year-old artist whose neighbors and subjects were the birds of Central Park, died on Sunday, September 27. Law enforcement sources told the New York Post that Rogers, who was unhoused, had been found beaten to death under the gazebo she called home, though the New York Police Department could not confirm the individual's identity to Hyperallergic due to the ongoing investigation. Rogers had become a fixture in the park as an avid birdwatcher and painter of its various locations, particularly in the Ramble, the heavily wooded section she frequented most often. "We used to call her the Grandma Moses of Central Park," Robert "Birding Bob" DeCandido told Hyperallergic in a phone interview, comparing the artist to the renowned folk landscape painter. "But she probably wouldn't want all this sympathy. She didn't call attention to herself."The artist reached Central Park through a difficult path, having gone by multiple names throughout her life. She was known as Elise Bainbridge Hill when she was the subject of Karen Gehres's 2007 documentary Begging Naked, in which she recounted running away from home as a teen, surviving as a sex worker, persevering through a heroin addiction, and finding space for her art in between.
